data.raw_text:
The Council on Geostrategy has updated its map of the AUKUS pact, which brings together the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia and is aimed at containing China and its proxies along the so-called CRINK axis — North Korea, Russia, and Iran.

Some additional key points have been added, for example in Africa and Venezuela; Greenland is also highlighted, and key military bases of the Chinese axis are marked.

As I wrote last time, this scheme clearly shows why the United States has been trying so hard (and will not abandon these efforts) to pull Russia out of China’s orbit and attach it to its own camp.

By doing so, Washington not only deprives China of cheap resources but also closes the ring from the north. The northern frontiers are precisely where Greenland comes into play, by the way.

Venezuela and Syria have already been taken away from China; now the U.S. will work on Iran, where the situation after the phase of protests has not improved — on the contrary, it has only worsened. 

This is an important point: time is working against the ayatollahs’ regime, and the protests — and the bloody way the regime crushed them — are quite literally symptoms.

The western and eastern barriers are not labeled that way by the Council on Geostrategy by accident — this is exactly how they are defined in U.S. military strategy. For example, the eastern barrier is the first line of defense formed by island chains, with South Korea at the tip of the spear.

The United States does not view Japan, Taiwan, or the Philippines separately, as individual states, but as parts of a single defensive architecture, while Australia is a crucial submarine base and the rear area for those very island-chain defensive lines.

And let us not forget that the U.S., the U.K., and Australia represent the peak of what human civilization currently offers: AI, space, technology, and, of course, forges of knowledge.

No joke — among the world’s top universities are — drumroll — MIT, Harvard, Oxford, Cambridge, the University of Melbourne, that is, precisely universities from the U.S., the U.K., and Australia.

And the fact that these very states (essentially sharing a single civilizational past rooted in Britain) are uniting into a single global defense pact — well, just a coincidence, you know, one of those coincidences that are simply coincidental.

In fact, no: all of this is interconnected and follows a clear pattern. And yes, China clearly understands its weak and defensive position, which is why it is not at all interested in ending the Russia–Ukraine war — that is, in easing direct pressure on the western perimeter.

Nor is it going to hand Russia over to the United States; it will cling to it to the very end — such a large piece is not given up freely or without a fight.

Overall, I would remind you that this also illustrates, among other things, why the United States ultimately did not abandon Ukraine — in short, because of the position of the United Kingdom, a position the Americans cannot ignore.

What I like about think tanks such as the Council on Geostrategy is their work in explaining the big picture: this map is an appendix to a multi-page report and helps to see the global context of what is happening.
